sections.h2: St. Mary's County at a glance
sections.html:
St. Mary's County sits on a peninsula at the southern tip of Southern Maryland, between the Patuxent, the Chesapeake Bay and the Potomac. The county seat is Leonardtown, and the 2020 population was 113,777. California, Lexington Park (13,317) and Leonardtown (4,745) are the main population centers, and Naval Air Station Patuxent River is by far the largest employer. About 73.2% of occupied homes are owner-occupied.

Water makes up 53% of the county's area, and the shoreline runs more than 500 miles. That matters when you sell, because coastal bluffs protect many areas from storm surge while low-lying land and tidal marshes are more exposed.

sections.h2: How property tax is assessed and billed
sections.html:
The State Department of Assessments and Taxation values the property. The St. Mary's County Treasurer sends and collects the bill at 23150 Leonard Hall Drive, Leonardtown, phone 301-475-4200, extension 3300.

The fiscal 2026 county real property rate is 0.8478. The county's tax bill estimator shows separate lines for county, state, fire tax, rescue and support, along with flat fees and a county homestead credit line, so the total depends on where the house sits.

Assessment topicRule
Reassessment cycleEvery three years, increase spread equally over three years
State cap on taxable increaseAnnual increase above 10% is not taxed; counties can set a lower cap
Appeal window45 days from the notice date
Next appeal levelsAppeals Board within 30 days, then Maryland Tax Court within 30 days

The county gets its tax file from the State on July 1, so ownership data updates once a year. Search by address or parcel number rather than by name.

The county holds its tax sale every year on the first Friday of March, covering the prior tax year. Owners of delinquent accounts are advertised in a local newspaper for four weeks before the sale.

The winning bidder receives a Certificate of Sale, which allows legal proceedings but carries no title or possession. If the owner redeems, the bidder gets back the taxes paid plus 6% annual interest through the month of redemption. If the owner does not redeem, the bidder may start court steps to foreclose the right to redeem. Properties are sold as is, and liens may survive the sale.

Treat the sale date as a hard deadline. Unpaid water and sewer bills, service charges and penalties are also first liens against the property, and MetCom handles those bills.

Expect the settlement company to pay off any property tax due at closing from your proceeds. The county posts bills and a payment portal online, and you can change a mailing address through the Treasurer's address change form.

If back taxes are close to the March sale, a cash offer with a quick closing can clear them. Compare it against a listing and ask for terms in writing. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal, which helps when time is short, but the lien still has to be paid before the deed is recorded.

Ask your settlement company about the county transfer and recordation taxes. State law limits St. Mary's County's transfer tax to 1%, with the first $30,000 of the buyer's principal residence price exempt, and part of the recordation tax revenue goes to rural land conservation. The company handling your closing will give you the rate in force.

A house on a private well or septic system has its own sale steps.

  • Under Maryland Real Property Section 10-713, a contract for a house with a private well must require water quality testing as a condition of sale. Results stay valid for three years, and the buyer can waive the test in writing.
  • Anyone performing a septic inspection for a property transfer has needed a license from the Board of On-Site Wastewater Professionals since July 1, 2022. Call the On-Site Systems Division at 410-537-3778 for county requirements.

Schedule both early. Test results and inspection reports take time, and they are often what holds up a closing on a rural or waterfront house.

If your house is near the water, check flood exposure and the condition of any bulkhead or shoreline structure before you set a price. Buyers and their inspectors will ask about both. Have the repair history and any documents ready, and tell buyers early what you know about storm damage or erosion at the shoreline.

Maryland Route 235 and Route 5 are the main state highways, with Routes 4, 6, 234 and 245 also serving the county. St. Mary's Transit runs local service, and the Maryland Transit Administration operates commuter bus service to Washington. About 20% of residents, 11,817 people, commute out of the county for work, so mention the commute options in a listing.

sections.h2: What to bring and what happens at closing
sections.html:
• The latest tax bill and any notice from the Treasurer.
  • Water and sewer account information, so MetCom balances can be checked.
  • The well test result and septic inspection report, if the house has them.
  • Records of work on a bulkhead or shoreline structure, for a waterfront house.

At settlement the title company collects the signed deed, pays the tax balance and any liens from your proceeds, and sends you the rest. Read the settlement statement before you sign. Compare the tax line with your latest bill, and ask the closing agent about any difference.

A cash buyer has no lender, so there is no appraisal to fail and no loan approval to wait on. The buyer may still inspect the house and run a title search. For a county house with a well, a septic system or a long repair list, that often means a firm closing date and fewer repair negotiations. What does not go away is the paperwork: well testing under Section 10-713 unless the buyer waives it in writing, any septic inspection the county requires, and payoff of every tax and utility lien.

If you inherited the house, confirm who has authority to sign before you talk to buyers. Several heirs can slow a closing more than price does. Line up every signature early, and keep the estate paperwork with your closing documents.

sections.h2: Steps for a St. Mary's County sale
sections.html:
1. Call the Treasurer for the current balance.
  2. Order the well test and septic inspection if the house has them.
  3. Check for unpaid MetCom water and sewer bills.
  4. Ask the settlement company for the transfer and recordation figures.
  5. Close, with taxes and liens paid from your proceeds.

faqs.q: What is the county seat of St. Mary's County?
faqs.a: Leonardtown is the county seat. California is the largest community, and Lexington Park is the other major population center near Naval Air Station Patuxent River.

faqs.q: What is the St. Mary's County property tax rate?
faqs.a: The fiscal 2026 county real property rate is 0.8478. Your bill also shows state, fire, rescue and support lines, so the total depends on where the house sits.

faqs.q: When is the St. Mary's County tax sale?
faqs.a: The county holds its annual tax sale on the first Friday of March for the prior tax year.

faqs.q: How do I appeal a St. Mary's County property assessment?
faqs.a: File within 45 days of the notice date with the local assessment office. Later levels are the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board and the Maryland Tax Court, each with a 30 day window.

faqs.q: Do I need to test the well before selling a St. Mary's County house?
faqs.a: If the house has a private well, Maryland Real Property Section 10-713 requires the contract to call for water testing as a condition of sale unless the buyer waives it in writing. Results are valid for three years.
